item.title: Review: Chuwi’s $449 Unibook laptop is a funhouse-mirror MacBook Neo
item.description:
The Unibook is a weird entry-level laptop for people with patience.

In another time, the MacBook Neo could have caused a substantial realignment of the lowish-end laptop business. Sure, it has shortcomings compared to the MacBook Air, but it could have at least encouraged PC makers to start shipping consistently decent keyboards, screens, and build quality in the Neo’s $599 price window.

The PC makers did start responding, thanks in part to Intel’sactually new non-Ultra Core Series 3 processors(codenamed Wildcat Lake). Intel has resisted its usual compunction to serve the budget market with aging, re-labeled silicon and has created a lower-end, lower-performance processor with the same building blocks (and the same manufacturing processes) as this year’s high-end, high-performance models.

The likes of Dell, Acer, Asus, and Lenovo began hopping on the Wildcat Lake train fairly quickly, announcing would-be Neo competitors. But it felt like most of them were having trouble matching the Neo’s barebones specs, let alone undercutting them. Dell’s XPS 13 started at $599, but only for students. Itwould be $699 for everyone else. Acer’s Swift Air 14was announced at $699, too. Sure, sometimes these offered features the Neo didn’t have. But thepointof the Neo is that it eschews frills and frippery in favor of nailing the basics.

But even the MacBook Neo ended up being too good to be true. Appleraised its price by $100three months after introducing it.

Yes, if you want a laptop that feels good, looks good, and performs well here in The Year Of The Unforgettable Memory Crisis, it’s hard to find a good deal, even if you’re willing to settle for a middle-shelf processor, the bare minimum amount of RAM that a modern operating system and browser will reasonably run on, and a meager 256GB or inexcessive 512GB storage drive.

There was one US-announced Wildcat Lake system thathasmanaged to undercut the MacBook Air and the rest of the industry, though. Chinese PC company Chuwi has put together theUnibook, a Wildcat Lake computer with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage that it’s selling for an introductory price of $449 (its “normal” price is listed at $569, but it’s not clear whether or when the price might go back up.)

On paper, that looks pretty good. And in practice, the Unibook isn’t completely without its charms. But “you get what you pay for” applies here in multiple ways, and it’s difficult to imagine recommending this machine to anyone other than a computer geek looking for a weird project PC.

The Unibook looks unassuming at first glance, somewhere in the neighborhood of an Asus Zenbook. It feels like a cop-out to describe something as “nondescript,” but this is a pretty down-the-middle clamshell PC design.

To begin with the good, the Unibook far outstrips the port offerings of the MacBook Neo or the new XPS 13. It offers a pair of USB-C ports, a full-size HDMI port, two 5Gbps USB 3 ports, one USB 2.0 port, a micro-SD card slot, a headphone jack, and even an Ethernet port. I’ve never loved the little folding-out design for Ethernet ports that some laptops use to save a little space—if and when the little hinge breaks, it will start flopping around and looking bad—but so many laptops use thin-and-lightness as an excuse to ship a bare-minimum allotment of ports that it’s nice to see a budget-minded laptop ship with a ton of connectivity options.

The Unibook’s M.2 2280 drive is also pretty easy to replace. Remove the 11 Philips-head screws on the bottom of the laptop, and its bottom pries up with a bit of pressure. If you want a larger drive or just one from a better-known company, it’s easy to put one in (the built-in SSD is made by “HOGE,” a name that means about as much to most North Americans as “Chuwi”). The Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module is also easily accessible; the battery is, too, if you can manage to find a replacement somehow.

Also in the “good” column is the laptop’s perfectly not-bad keyboard. The keys aren’t as firm or satisfying as those on the keyboards in the MacBook lineup or in Framework’s Laptop 12 or Laptop 13, but the typing feel is decent, and the backlight is nice and even. The computer is missing a fingerprint reader (there’s also no face-scanning camera, which means the Unibook has no biometric login option at all), but this is a corner that the MacBook Neo’s base model also cuts.

Judged by the standards of the category, the Unibook’s screen isn’t awful. It’s a 13-inch IPS display panel with a decent 1920 x 1200 resolution and 16:10 aspect ratio, a step up from the 16:9 1080p displays you’ll still find in some ultra-budget systems. But it’s also not very nice by the MacBook Neo’s standards: only 300-ish nits of maximum brightness, pretty noticeable backlight bleeding around the edges (at least on our unit), and around 59 percent coverage of the sRGB color gamut, according to my colorimeter. At that level, colors appear visibly faded or washed-out to the naked eye; I find it particularly noticeable with shades of red and purple.

The mediocre screen was an unpleasant surprise given that this thing advertised 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage when it was announced and on its product page for many weeks (the Internet Archive captures ithere). But since then, the company has said that onlya higher-specced Unibook 315actually has a screen with 100 percent sRGB gamut coverage, in addition to an extra P-core on the CPU, 12GB of RAM instead of 8GB, and a 512GB SSD. You still can’t buy this version of the Unibook, though Chuwi says it “may” be available this month and it “may” cost $599.

I run out of nice things to say about the Unibook after the screen. The webcam is usable, insofar as it functions, but the image quality is fuzzy, and it has trouble with white balance. The speakers produce sound under some circumstances (more on that later).

The trackpad is probably the worst of the Unibook’s core features. The actual finger tracking is OK, one gift of the precision trackpad era that endures despite the hardware’s shortcomings. Aside from that, it’s awful—it’s stiff. It’s hard to click. It’s so, so loud. It’s a trackpad that makes you glad for tap-to-click. It’s almost bad enough to ruin the laptop all by itself, though it does have some other help.

When you buy a no-name PC, part of what you have to assume is that you areessentiallyout in the cold with respect to aftermarket software support. Maybe you’ll get some driver and/or BIOS updates directly from the manufacturer, and maybe you won’t! But you should assume that you won’t, and you should assume that whatever driver support page exists might be busted or deleted at pretty much any time. The driver page for the Unibook has not worked even once at any point during the weeks I’ve been using it.

Usually this means putting up with things that feel just a littleoffor downright weird, like a BIOS that seems to expose every possible setting whether it’s necessary or not, a shortcut to a Windows 7-era Control Panel applet sitting on the desktop by default for some reason, or the system’s pre-installed Microsoft Office 2024 suite.

If you think it’s odd that a $449 computer would come with Microsoft Office pre-installed or that it’s even more odd that Chuwi doesn’t advertise pre-installed Microsoft Office, you’re right. The copy installed on our review unit was definitely activated using a common activation script, something I verified by running the script and checking Office’s activation status.

Security-wise, the Windows installseemsto check out, insofar as it meets Windows 11’s Security dashboard’s “enhanced security” baseline (at least, it did after a round of updates and a reboot). Chinese PC makers will occasionally ship a driver, inadvertently or otherwise, that comes with malware on board, so it’s something you need to watch for.

What the Unibookdoesship with is all kinds of weird little Microsoft bits and bobs that don’t come with a clean-from-USB Windows 11 install, including a “mobile plans” app (the laptop has no modem, and the app opens to a blank window that does nothing), and the obscure “Microsoft PC Manager” app. The only page I can find for iton what is apparently Microsoft’s actual websiteis full of bizarre, possibly auto-translated sentence fragments like “Cleanup your system and free up spaces” and “Enhance the efficiency of computer use”). Some Chinese language packs are also preinstalled.

Normally, I’d treat this sort of PC the same as I’d treat most computers from most OEMs: Blow away the stock Windows installation and control my own destiny. Sure, a “clean” install of Windows 11 isn’t the cruft-removal magic wand that it used to be, but it’s still a good way to make sure you’re dealing mainly with Microsoft’s nonsense and not additional manufacturer-added nonsense on top of that.

For the Unibook, this wasn’t smooth sailing.

As you saw earlier in this review, Chuwi’s support site is currently suffering from an acute case of “Database Working Un-normal.” This made downloading drivers pretty difficult, partly because Wildcat Lake is new enough that Windows Update doesn’t seem to have drivers ready to go.

As a precaution, I replaced the Unibook’s drive with a spare 256GB SSD I had pulled from some other laptop at some point. When I ran into problems getting some of the hardware to work, I switched back to the old SSD andused Windows’ built-in DISM servicing toolto export every single third-party driver installed on the system.

If you need to reinstall drivers onto the Unibookwithoutthe benefit of a backup from the existing system, this patchwork also seemed to clear all the exclamation points from the Device Manager:

But even with a nice, clean Device Manager, sound still wasn’t coming out of the Unibook’s speakers—it didn’t even see that an audio output was installed. By diving into the “System devices” section and selecting a generic audio controller driver, I was able to install an “Intel Smart Sound Technology Bus” device that finally seemed to make Windows recognize the remainder of the not-installed audio drivers, which got everything working again.

For your convenience, I am also including the pile of audio drivers I extracted from the Unibook’s default Windows installhere.

The audio problem was also present in Linux, when I tried Kubuntu 26.04 LTS on the system. In addition, the laptop wouldn’t go to sleep when its lid was closed, which put a pretty good dent in the battery life. Some othershave had some successgetting this stuff working, but it wasn’t something I spent much time on for this review.

Wildcat Lake is Intel’s first genuinely compelling low-end laptop processor in quite a while.

It used to be standard for lower-end laptop CPUs to be cut-down versions of high-end ones, based on the same architecture and manufacturing process. But as manufacturing improvements have gotten harder to do, Intel (and others) have turned to rebranded previous-generation chips to serve more budget-minded systems. Intel’s 12th- and 13th-generation Core processors weren’t especially impressive laptop chips in the first place (mediocre battery life; same GPU as 11th-generation), and getting warmed over and returned to market as theCore Series 1andCore Series 2families didn’t make them any better.

Wildcat Lake only has one or two P-cores (one for this version of the Unibook), four E-cores, and one or two GPU execution units. But they at least benefit from being built on the same architectures as the Panther Lake Core Ultra Series 3 processors, including the Intel 18A process for the main CPU die.

Objectively, performance is not impressive. But even a single P-core means a much faster and snappier-feeling computer than you’d get if you used one of Intel’s all-E-cores budget processors, and the Core 3 304 chip is perfectly serviceable for browsing, communicating, or streaming video. The comparison to Apple’s A18 Pro, the MacBook Neo’s chip, isn’t especially flattering for Intel—the Core 3 304 has one fewer P-core and higher power consumption, which means its performance-per-Watt for heavy tasks is pretty bad (it doesn’t use a ton of power, but it takes a very long time, so overall efficiency for these tasks isn’t great.) The Core 3 304’s single-core GPU also looks pretty bad next to the A18 Pro’s.

If you were hoping to play games or edit photos or video, the other blocker is the 8GB allotment of RAM, which was little enough that it kept benchmarks like Cinebench 2024, Cinebench 2026, or many GPU benchmarks from running entirely.

But its saving grace is its battery life—because it uses newer manufacturing tech, Wildcat Lake enables the Unibook’s 53 WHr battery to last for nearly 15 hours while running the PCMark Modern Office benchmark with the screen brightness set to 200 nits. That’s more than enough to make it through a full day away from an outlet.

If a computer’s price in 2026 seems too good to be true, it probably is—Chuwi’s Unibook is interesting, but I’d hesitate to recommend it as a primary laptop to pretty much anybody. Some of that comes down to the hardware—mainly the awful trackpad, but also the worse-than-expected screen—and some of it is that you’ll be mostly on your own for hardware and software support after you buy it. A MacBook Neo or even the new Dell XPS might be more expensive, but at least you’ll have someone to call if something goes wrong.

And that’s before you get to the actual specs. The Unibookisa decent showcase for Intel’s Core Series 3 processors, which offer pretty stellar battery life, along with performance that’s more than good enough for basic computing. But 8GB of RAM will severely limit the kinds of apps that run well (or run at all) on a PC, and trying to play anything other than basic 2D games on a laptop like this won’t go well.

item.title: Trump tried to curb clean energy. It’s booming anyway.
item.description:
Capacity will rise by a record 45GW this year, according to S&P Global Energy.

Donald Trump is presiding over an unexpected clean energy boom, as rising electricity demand spurs investment in new capacity despite the US administration’s efforts to thwart a solar and wind rollout.

Clean energy additions will rise by a record 45 gigawatts this year, according to S&P Global Energy—equivalent to the average electricity demand of Turkey. The increase is roughly 25 percent higher than the record set in 2024.

The US president’s war in Iran, which has driven up global energy prices, along with surging power demand from AI data centers and developers’ rush to capitalize on expiring tax credits, are driving the cleantech boom, said analysts. Trump’s administration has also been pragmatic in the face of its energy needs.

“There was a campaign promise to go against renewables, but at the same time they’re realizing that you can’t do without it,” said Izzet Bensusan, chief executive of Captona, an energy infrastructure investment group. “I don’t see a world where power demand is flattening out.”

S&P said new solar and wind capacity will jump in 2026 by nearly a third and almost 50 percent respectively. Solar will set another record in 2027, while wind falls back before recovering.

White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers, however, touted “record-high oil and gas production” under Trump.

“The president has delivered on his promise to unleash American energy,” Rogers said. “At the same time, the administration has ended subsidies for costly and unreliable energy sources that American taxpayers were unfairly forced to fund.”

The solar and wind additions come despite Trump’s early efforts to kill an energy transition pushed by his predecessor, Joe Biden.

The Trump administration broke up Esmeralda 7 in Nevada. It would have been the largest single solar project in the US.

The president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act also slashed tax credits for solar and wind, and his administration has interfered with routine project approvals, including for more than 150 onshore wind projects. But under the terms of the OBBBA, solar and wind developers had until July 4 to begin work on projects and until 2030 to finish them.

The deadline “prompted developers to hurry and begin construction,” said S&P Global renewables analyst John Murray.

Expectations for sharply higher electricity demand are also driving the pace of the rollout.

US power consumption is expected to grow 39 percent by 2035, according to consultancy ICF, driven by energy-hungry data centers and the electrification of household appliances and transport. The surge comes after demand remained steady for more than a decade.

Solar and wind are among the quickest, cheapest forms of energy to add to the grid. According to RMI, a think-tank, new solar and wind sites have a lead time of less than two years, compared to at least three years to develop gas projects.

Producers can break even by selling solar and wind power for as little as $38 and $37 per megawatt-hour, respectively, compared to at least $48 per megawatt-hour for gas, according to investment bank Lazard. However, these figures do not fully account for system upgrade costs and batteries to smooth out intermittency.

Renewable power developers also stand to profit, as electricity prices are expected to rise 40 to 120 percent once Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act subsidies expire.

“Candidly, it’s a good time to be a developer,” said Ethan Zindler, head of country and policy research at BloombergNEF. “Data centers need power, and they need it basically yesterday.”

Extreme weather and Trump’s Iran war have also contributed to the growth.

Consumer investment in residential solar panels, batteries, and zero-emission vehicles led clean energy spending in the second quarter of 2026, increasing 45 percent from the previous quarter and 21 percent from the same period in 2025, according to researcher Rhodium Group.

“People in Florida are installing a lot of home batteries to ensure their house still has power in a hurricane,” said Hannah Hess, a director with Rhodium’s energy and climate practice. “And with the Iran war driving higher fuel prices, we’re seeing more EV and hybrid [vehicle] purchasing.”

US courts have slowed Trump’s war on green energy. A district court judge in Oregon recently ordered the Pentagon to cease blocking onshore wind development. The courts have blocked all five of the administration’s attempts to halt construction at wind projects off the US’s East Coast.

Developers are having some success lobbying the administration directly, leaning on people with ties to the administration to advocate for individual projects, people familiar told the FT. Among the arguments is that the projects will not displace fossil fuels—Trump’s preferred source of energy.

“What we found on the permit side is that the administration is pretty pragmatic,” said Cliff Graham, chief executive at clean energy company Avantus. “There’s a lot of land between Reno, Tucson, and Barstow, where there’s no better use than solar-plus-storage.”

item.title: F1 in the Netherlands: The driver you most want to beat is your teammate
item.description:
Formula 1 returned from its summer break with this weekend’s Dutch Grand Prix.

After months of rumors surrounding his future, now we know: Four-time champion Max Verstappen is staying in the sport for the foreseeable future. The news broke on the eve of the Dutch Grand Prix, held this past weekend at Zandvoort in the Netherlands as F1 returned from its mandatory summer vacation.

Verstappen’s wasn’t the only contract news—Williams will keep both Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz, too. More than once I’ve noticed a driver having an underwhelming weekend following a freshly signed contract; in this case, all three had a weekend they’d probably rather forget. They weren’t the only ones, though. Up and down the grid, we saw friction between teammates. And there’s no one an F1 driver wants to beat more than the only other person to have the same car as they do.

Formula 1 returned from its summer break with this weekend’s Dutch Grand Prix.

One of the things that sets F1 apart from most other disciplines in motorsport is the constant in-season development of the cars. A team might start the year with the best car and a commanding advantage over its rivals, but others can and will catch up. The 2009 season is a good example of this; Brawn GP started the year with at least a second a lap in hand over the rest of the grid, and Jenson Button built up a big early lead in the championship after winning five of the first six races.

That was the last race he’d win all year. The team was operating on a shoestring budget and simply couldn’t afford to upgrade its car. Button’s teammate Rubens Barrichello would win two more races for Brawn that year, but by year’s end, Red Bull and McLaren had both caught up with, then eclipsed, Brawn’s pace. The following year, Brawn GP was bought by Mercedes, the money spigot turned on, and, once the hybrid era began in 2014, the championships started flowing.

Ironically, there might be a danger of something similar happening again. After never really getting a handle on the ground effect regulations (2022–2025), Mercedes put a lot of effort into starting the 2026 rule set as it did in 2014, with the most powerful hybrid power units and a chassis that could exploit them. And it did, winning the first six races in a row. But the car has been plagued with unreliability, most of it affecting George Russell and not Kimi Antonelli (who now, like Button in 2009, has a commanding lead over everyone else in the driver’s championship).

And unlike in 2014, Mercedes can’t just throw money at the problem. F1 teams now operate under a strict cost cap of $215 million (plus a little extra if they’re permitted an engine upgradeas was announced in Monaco), and this weekend Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff told journalists, “We haven’t got the money to put developments on the car. I said before that we are trying to evenly split that through the season based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimizing the championship points. But we just can’t do what we can’t do.”

Indeed, at Zandvoort, Mercedes was fast, but so too was McLaren, which has now proven its ability to bring upgrades to the track that work as intended across both the ground effect era and now this one. And in the hands of Lando Norris, the orange-and-black McLaren was fast enough to hunt down and pass Antonelli before winning by almost 12 seconds.

Alpine brought plenty of upgrades to Zandvoort, as did Ferrari and McLaren. And at Hungary, just before the break, Aston Martin finally dragged itself into the midpack. A Honda engine upgrade arrived this weekend that has helped close the gap a little more. Fernando Alonso told journalists that “we used to be 4.5 seconds average on the gap to the leader, so we improved three seconds in two races,” and the veteran driver finished in the points for the second time, coming home on Sunday in ninth place. But Honda still has work to do, according to Alonso’s teammate Lance Stroll, who complained about poor drivability and a gearbox that would sometimes reject instructions to downshift.

An F1 driver’s most direct measure of performance is the person on the other side of the garage. Which means that intra-team dynamics can often get fractious. Relations between Albon and Sainz at Williams actually seem rather good, at least from the outside, but it didn’t stop the pair from colliding after Sainz got unsettled by a bump and locked his brakes while the two cars were side by side, ending Albon’s race.

The Audi pair almost had a similar problem when Gabriel Bortoleto spun on a greasy but drying track that also caught out and wrecked Verstappen on the opening lap. Quick reactions by Nico Hulkenberg meant the silver, red, and black cars did not exchange paint.

Other driver pairings were less pleased with each other. Russell was told to move over for Antonelli on lap 65 as Mercedes figured the young championship leader had a better chance of beating Norris’ McLaren. But the Mercedes finished second and third, with Antonelli ahead and now with an even greater lead—59 points—over Russell.

Lewis Hamilton is also 59 points behind Antonelli, having finished fourth ahead of his teammate at Ferrari, Charles Leclerc. Like Mercedes, Ferrari issued team orders, instructing Leclerc to pit so Hamilton, who was on a different strategy, could maximize the use of his tires. But Leclerc stayed out for several laps, aggravating Hamilton in the process. “Great way of wasting time guys, good job,” Hamilton told the team over the radio.

F1 now heads off to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in a couple of weeks, as do I, but there might not be a race report, as this time it’s an actual vacation.

]]>

item.title: Nvidia senior manager linked to Supermicro scheme smuggling AI servers to China
item.description:
Nvidia worker indicted after Jensen Huang scolded Supermicro for AI server smuggling.

Taiwan has indicted nine people—reportedlyincluding an Nvidia senior manager and two Supermicro employees based in the country—who allegedly helped forge documents to cover up illegal exports of high-end AI servers to China in violation of US export controls.

On Monday, Reutersreportedthat prosecutors in Keelung did not release any names but confirmed that the suspects were “charged with breach of trust and document forgery.” One suspect linked to a related case remains at large, accused of the “siphoning of funds from a distributor company involved” in helping China get access to restricted Nvidia chips.

Since 2022, the US has required a license to export semiconductors to China, with the intent of protecting national security by staying ahead of China in the AI race. But after the USarrestedSupermicro co-founder Wally Liaw in March for allegedly funneling $2.5 billion in restricted AI servers to China since 2024, Taiwan launched a separate probe to learn more about the scheme.

Taiwan’s investigation found that co-conspirators attempted to falsify documents to make it appear that 130 B300 servers were installed and in use at a Taiwan facility. But 74 of those servers “were ultimately exported and delivered to Chinese customers,” Reuters reported, while the rest, 56, were intended to go to China but were blocked once Taiwanese customs officials “detected irregularities.”

Ars could not reach Supermicro or Nvidia for comment.

In a statementto PC Mag, Supermicro has previously confirmed that it’s cooperating with Taiwanese investigators.

“Supermicro is committed to protecting our advanced technologies and intellectual property. We are working closely with Taiwanese authorities on recent events, which underscore the importance of continued collaboration across industry and government to strengthen safeguards, enhance supply chain visibility, and facilitate the enforcement of export control laws,” Supermicro said.

The firm is not a target of the probe, Supermicro emphasized, which so far has targeted at least 12 locations to uncover suspected smugglers. Although US employees are believed to be integral to the scheme, Lauren Barden-Hair, an expert in China’s power over multinational firms across Southeast Asia, posted an op-ed in The Hill,notingthat the US found that “a nameless Southeast Asian firm” was “at the heart of the operation.” That firm allegedly coordinated with co-conspirators at Supermicro and Nvidia, succeeding for years at ensuring that China wasn’t completely blocked from accessing Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

Both US firms will likely need to assess the steps they take to comply with US export controls. In May, before any Nvidia employees were linked directly to the scheme, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was highly critical of Supermicro for its failing compliance program, urging that a fix was needed, Tom’s Hardwarereported.

“We insist our partners are compliant. We hope that they will enhance and improve their regulation compliance and prevent that from happening in the future,” Huang said at the time.

Supermicro has confirmed that it has already made changes. It also fired several employees that an internal investigation connected to the Chinese AI server scheme, Tom’s Hardwarereported. Conducted by a third party, that probe cleared Supermicro’s current senior officials of any involvement. However, the company may have been neglectful in not noticing that “billions of dollars’ worth of hardware was being sent to questionable clients,” Tom’s Hardware noted. Spooked investors have even sued Supermicro for securities fraud, fearing that the company’s sales may be dominated by such illicit sales.

Taiwanese prosecutors said that all employees indicted were “fully aware” that Nvidia and Supermicro have “rigorous internal control procedures” regarding exports to China, Reuters reported. The US and Taiwan have recently tightened those controls, prosecutors said, yet employees’ scheme only got more brazen, Barden-Hair’s op-ed suggested. Supermicro’s team allegedly was so confident that it could evade US and Taiwanese export controls that it made “increasingly daring deals” to get China the computing power it wanted.

Taiwan officials announced that they recently uncovered more of the same misconduct. They alleged that Nvidia’s manager and Supermicro employees “colluded with one another at various levels for enormous profit, illegally exporting high-end servers, increasing corporate compliance costs, and severely damaging our nation’s international image,” Taiwan authorities said Monday.

The US is determined to cut off China’s access to Nvidia’s AI chips and servers, and it seems to be taking a two-prong approach to tighten controls even further.

First, lawmakers are weighing a bill called the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would allow US export controls to extend to include remote cloud-based access to critical hardware and software, CNBCreported.

Passing that law would allow rule-making that could cut China off from exploiting a known loophole that currently impedes the US from interfering with its remote access to Nvidia chips via data centers in Southeast Asia. According to industry experts, remote access to computing power is a key factor driving Chinese models’ capability gains for companies including Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent, CNBC reported. And China will apparently soon have more data centers nearby to potentially expand remote access to compute, as hyperscalers plan to multiply the number of facilities in the region, leaping from two data centers today to 31 planned projects underway.

That bill will likely face industry pushback, CNBC suggested, since cloud providers would bear the cost of that new compliance regime, including implementing better know-your-customer protocols.

For the US, ending remote access may seem like an increasingly urgent priority, but the Supermicro scandal shows that evading controls can often be as easy as forging a document in an overburdened system where neither top executives nor customs officials managed to flag billions of dollars in fraudulent diversions.

However, the global crackdown on employees who are striking shady deals to export AI servers to China does come as Nvidia recently announcedit’s increasing the prices of AI servers by 15 percent. So, at the very least, any employees motivated by the potential of gaining even higher profits from illicit sales will seemingly be on notice.

In her op-ed, Barden-Hair suggested that the US was blindsided by Chinese AI server smuggling because it failed to learn from its own history. In 1998, the Senate Committee on Governmental Affairsinvestigated“Chinagate,” a campaign finance scandal where China used Southeast Asian companies as a cover to try to influence election outcomes.

In that scheme, China learned that cultivating ties with business moguls—particularly those who had deep financial investments in China but were based just outside its sovereign territory—provided the “ideal cover,” Barden-Hair said. And similarly, the unnamed Southeast Asian firm at the heart of the Supermicro scandal appears to follow the same playbook, she said.

“It is easy to point out errors in judgment after a disaster, and US export control authorities deserve support and praise for their efforts to protect national security,” Barden-Hair said. “But it is important that we take the right lessons from the Supermicro scandal amid our shaming of the guilty, and remember the hard-earned lessons of the past. With the anonymous company the Justice Department refers to, China is showing us, again, that its pawns are scattered beyond its borders, and that its financial tentacles have a real and devastating influence.”

item.title: Buyer beware: Those mummified remains might carry toxic spores
item.description:
“Mummified remains sold online exhibit signs of biodeterioration, yet sellers provide no safety guidance.”

Mummified human and animal remains have long been in demand among collectors, and such items are sufficiently rare that their acquisition may involve unregulated, occasionally clandestine trade practices—if not outright illegal ones. According to the authors ofa paperpublished in the International Journal of Cultural Property, the risks to would-be collectors aren’t just legal. Mummified remains may also pose a significant health hazard due to toxic substances used in their preservation and microbial growth due to improper storage. In fact, toxic spores or fungi are often cited as the source of the legendary “mummy’s curse” tied to the excavation of King Tutankhamen’s tomb.

Per the authors, the mummification process throughout history has relied on various toxic materials and substances to help preserve the remains—heavy metals like arsenic, mercury, and lead, for example—which is why careful handling is necessary to avoid adverse health effects. (Professionals typically don masks, gloves, and lab coats when working with such remains.) Various micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi, yeasts) can also lie dormant in the tissues for centuries and can recolonize and multiply due to a ready supply of organic material—particularly if the remains have been stored in suboptimal conditions.

A1962 case, for example, revealed the presence of poisonous fungi spores in mummified remains that would cause respiratory inflammation and infection if inhaled, as well as fever. A2013 studyfound that the hundreds of mummies on display at the Capuchin Catacombs in Palermo, Sicily, are prone to microbial and fungal growth after years of unstable environmental conditions. Similarly,in 2012, scientists identified three species of fungi (Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Stachybotrys) on human remains, coffins, walls, and in the air in the crypts of the Church of St. Peter and Paul in Krakow, Poland.

These microorganisms can have serious health effects. Spores ofAspergillus flavusfamouslyinfected and killed10 of the 12 scientists who first opened the 15th century Royal tomb of Grand Duke Casimir IV Jagillon in Poland in 1973. Rumors of a “mummy’s curse” have also dogged the death ofGeorge Herbert, fifth Earl of Carnarvon, who funded Howard Carter’s expedition that discovered Tutankhamen’s tomb. The theory that Lord Carnarvonsuccumbed to exposureto toxic fungi—one archaeologist reported seeing a black fungus inside the tomb—was dismissed outright as “tommy-rot” by Carter, who had asked a scientist to test the bandages for any pathogens.

Carnarvon died after accidentally slashing a fresh mosquito bite while shaving; it became infected, and he died of blood poisoning—technically pneumonia arising from a streptococcal infection of the skin, according to a1994 reportpublished in The Lancet. Carnarvon had long been prone to chronic lung infections. Per The Lancet article, there was a “general belief that one acute attack of bronchitis could have killed him.” In fact, 58 people were present when King Tut’s tomb was opened, and only eight died within 12 years. Lord Carnarvon’s daughter, Lady Evelyn Herbert, was among the first to enter, and she didn’t die until 1980. That hasn’t stopped the “mummy’s curse” story from resurfacing occasionally, most recently in a2022 documentarythat cited the toxic spores theory.

All that microbial growth still poses a serious health risk to collectors of mummified remains. “The rise of the Internet, especially social media, has amplified international trafficking and driven demand for unique cultural heritage, including mummified humans and animals,”said co-author Kirsty Squiresof the University of Staffordshire. “However, these preserved remains pose health and biosecurity risks, due to the toxicity of embalming methods and/or suboptimal storage that can promote microbial growth. Our research revealed that mummified remains sold online exhibit signs of biodeterioration, yet sellers provide no safety guidance, suggesting limited awareness or deliberate disregard of hazards.”

Squires et al. scoured the Internet for public posts related to the sale or collection of mummified remains, both human and animal: public and business pages on Facebook, public Instagram pages, websites of brick-and-mortar stores, a Dutch e-commerce platform, and online auctioneers. Only 24 of the 128 posts included in the study came from non-Meta platforms. All the posts were anonymized to protect any personal information, although unaltered versions were stored on an external hard drive not connected to the cloud.

Most of the items for sale were mummified human remains, usually body parts such as hands and feet, or heads (like Peruvian shrunken heads); six were animals, specifically a cat, a falcon, an ibis, a perch, and a primate skull. Only one seller was offering a complete mummified body. The authors note that such items are extremely rare and hence very costly; such transactions would not usually be handled via public social media posts.

The resulting analysis showed that sellers were very much aware of any legal issues associated with the sale and shipment of mummified human remains, often specifying geographical locations where laws forbid such transfers. Typically, such sellers would not openly declare shipment contents to avoid seizure by authorities. There was also often no provenance offered for such items.

The authors were particularly alarmed to note 13 Facebook posts offering mummified remains with visible fungal colonization in the photos, likely due to improper storage conditions: yellow spots, white spots, white spots on a black patina, white and gray spots, black and pink patinas, and so forth. Because such growth is not always immediately visible to the naked eye, the problem may be widespread.

“There is evidence to show that mummified remains are being mailed to buyers, both nationally and internationally, with little (if any) consideration of the health and safety implications of these actions,”said Squires. “Clearer, more prominent guidelines are needed to ensure buyers and sellers are unable to misinterpret or find loopholes in shipping policies.”

International Journal of Cultural Property, 2026. DOI:10.1017/S0940739126100393(About DOIs).

item.title: Inaudible sounds used to fingerprint browsers catch AliExpress red-handed
item.description:
Is the technique outdated? Yes. Is it still creepy? Also yes.

Chinese retailer AliExpress has been caught fingerprinting visitors after one of the metrics—an outdated technique that measures inaudible sounds it sends to browsers—impeded a researcher’s ability to use his bluetooth headphones.

Researcher Matthew Callaghansaidhe stumbled on the stealthy tracking by mistake. After loading the AliExpress homepage, audio from his phone stopped playing over his multipoint headphones, which accept connections from more than one device at a time. He set the headphones to play sounds from his phone except when his PC was producing audio. Each time he loaded AliExpress, the phone audio stopped. Each time he closed the tab the site was loaded into, the phone was once again audible.

While investigating the odd behavior, Callaghan said he found two highly obfuscated scripts. Together, they rendered a graph that analyzed theWebAudioreadings of each visiting browser. This graph acted as an oscillator that measuredSawtooth waves, which are common in output from digital audio.

“The oscillator generates a known waveform,” Callaghan wrote. “The analyser measures the result after it has passed through the browser’s audio implementation, and the script reads frequency data from it.”

The scripts set the gain to zero to prevent users from hearing anything. But because the graph is still connected to the selected system audio, the browser continues to process it and, eventually, sends it to AliExpress.

Variability in different math libraries, which are used when audio is produced through browsers, were once high enough to provide a massively large number of uniquely different signatures when combined with different CPUs and other system differences. After the audio soundprinting technique became well known, Firefox implemented a fix, starting inversion 118released in 2023. Beginningthen, the browser used its own unique math libraries, rather than relying on ones that shipped with the OS it ran on. Tom Ritter, a Firefox developer who has also volunteered for the Tor Project,saidthe move to constant libraries reduced the entropy enough to stop the technique from working.

The technique is ineffective in Chrome because it, too, ships with its own libraries, a Google spokesperson said. Safari users are likely safe for the same reason, although Apple didn’t immediately confirm that.

AliExpress’ use of an obsolete fingerprinting method raises the question: Why is it bothering to use it? The likely answer has to do with the more than a dozen other fingerprinting methods the online retailer is using. Callaghan said the other techniques included:

It’s likely the web audio trick is left over from years earlier and no one noticed it until now.

It’s comforting to know that browser makers have taken precautions. At the same time, it’s not yet clear how effective the rest of the metrics AliExpress is using are. Less reassuring still: it’s almost a certainty that thousands of sites are employing similar tracking. Browser developers are in a dynamic race with site publishers, who are constantly looking for new ways to break the latest protections.

item.title: GM vehicles under federal scrutiny after hundreds of reports
item.description:
The eBoost brake-by-wire system is responsible for at least 22 crashes now.

The federal government isexpanding a safety investigationinto a number of vehicles manufactured by General Motors after receiving hundreds of reports of brake failure. The problem affects more than 1.1 million cars, including many of GM’s electric vehicles, as well as ones it has built for Honda and Acura. The problem is with the brake-by-wire system (which GM callseBoost), which can suffer a spindle fracture while driving.

GM says that in the event of that happening, the car should still retain a number of critical safety features—antilock brakes, traction control, and stability control—at least until it comes to a complete stop, at which point they become inoperable. But NHTSA’s ODI says that it has received many reports that contradict this behavior and allege that eBoost failures are followed by an immediate loss of braking, which obviously poses a safety risk.

Indeed, NHTSA has received 227 incident reports, a number that grows to 745 once you include the hundreds of occurrences reported to GM. Twenty-two cases resulted in crashes, and while six people have been injured in five crashes, thankfully there have been no fatal incidents.

NHTSA says that the following vehicles are equipped with eBoost: “2023-2026 MY Cadillac Lyriq, Chevrolet Colorado, and GMC Canyon; 2024-2026 MY Buick Enclave, Envision; Chevrolet Blazer EV, Equinox EV, Traverse; Cruise Origin; and GMC Acadia; 2025-2026 MY Cadillac Celestiq and Optiq. ODI is also aware of 2024-2026 MY Acura ZDX and 2024-2026 MY Honda Prologue vehicles that were built with this system.”
